{{ill|Akiyama clan|en|Akiyama clan|WD=Q2975207|lt=Akiyama clan|1=Akiyama clan}} }} The '''{{nihongo|Takeda Clan|武田氏|Takeda-shi}}''' was a Japanese {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} clan active from the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} until the late 16th century. The clan was historically based in {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}} in present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|WD=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}}.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Kokushi Daijiten (国史大辞典) | title = Takeda-shi (武田氏) | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-09 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | language = Japanese | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }}{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Takeda family | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} The clan reached its greatest influence under the rule of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen|1=Takeda Shingen}}, one of the most famous rulers of the period. ==History== ===Origin=== [[File:Yōshū Chikanobu Shiragi Saburo and Tokiaki.jpg|thumb|right|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu was famous in horsemanship and archery, here playing the musical instrument {{ill|Shō (instrument)|en|Shō (instrument)|WD=Q1975355|lt=shō|1=Shō (instrument)}}]] The Takeda are descendants of the {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa|1=Emperor Seiwa}} (858–876), the 56th Emperor of Japan, and are a branch of the [[Minamoto clan]] ({{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji|1=Seiwa Genji}}), by {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|WD=Q3083118|lt=Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|1=Minamoto no Yoshimitsu}} (1056–1127), son of the ''[[:en:Chinjufu-shōgun|Chinjufu-shōgun]]'' [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988-1075), and brother to the famous {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie|1=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} (1039–1106).{{Cite book|last=Hubbard|first=Ben|title=Samurai Warriors|publisher=Cavendish Square Publishing, LLC|year=2017|isbn=978-1-5026-2459-8|location=New York, NY|pages=64}}{{Cite book|last=Shaw|first=Scott|title=Hapkido: Korean Art of Self-Defense|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4629-0344-3|language=en}} {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|en|Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|WD=Q6863154|lt=Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|1=Minamoto no Yoshikiyo}} (1075–1149), son of Yoshimitsu, was the first to take the name of Takeda, which he took when his father granted him Takeda domain in {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|WD=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi Province|1=Hitachi Province}}; thereafter, he was known as Takeda Yoshikiyo. ===Kamakura to early Azuchi–Momoyama periods=== In the 12th century, at the end of the Heian period, the Takeda family-controlled {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}}. Along with a number of other families, they supported their cousin [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] against the [[Taira clan|Taira]] clan in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War|1=Genpei War}} (1180–85). When Yoritomo was first defeated at Ishibashiyama (1181), {{ill|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|en|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|WD=Q7392303|lt=Takeda Nobuyoshi|1=Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)}} (1128–86) was applied for help, and the Takeda sent an army of 25,000 soldiers to support Yoritomo. Takeda Nobumitsu (1162–1248), son of Nobuyoshi, fought against the Taira, against {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|en|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|WD=Q1139202|lt=Kiso Yoshinaka|1=Minamoto no Yoshinaka}} (1184), distinguished himself in the [[:en:Battle of Ichinotani|Battle of Ichinotani]] (1184), and was appointed ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' (Governor) of Kai province. He also fought against the {{ill|Northern Fujiwara|en|Northern Fujiwara|WD=Q1050942|lt=Northern Fujiwara|1=Northern Fujiwara}} (1189) and against {{ill|Wada Yoshimori|en|Wada Yoshimori|WD=Q3564968|lt=Wada Yoshimori|1=Wada Yoshimori}} (1213). During the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}}, he helped the {{ill|Hōjō clan|en|Hōjō clan|WD=Q834364|lt=Hōjō|1=Hōjō clan}}, and led 50,000 soldiers as 'Daishōgun of the Tosando' , and in reward received the governorship of Aki province (1221). Takeda Nobuhide (1413–40), eldest son of the Takeda Nobushige (1390–1465), Shugo of Aki, helped the 6th shogun {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshinori|en|Ashikaga Yoshinori|WD=Q239170|lt=Ashikaga Yoshinori|1=Ashikaga Yoshinori}} (1394–1441) against the revolt of Isshiki Yoshitsura and was granted the governorship of Wakasa province (1440). Takeda Nobukata (1420–71) inherited the titles of Shugo of Wakasa from his brother Nobuhide, and that of Shugo of Aki from his father Nobushige. During the {{ill|Ōnin War|en|Ōnin War|WD=Q385676|lt=Ōnin War|1=Ōnin War}} (1467–77) he occupied Tango province that belonged to Isshiki Yoshinao and received the governorship of Tango province (1469). His brother Takeda Kuninobu (1437–90) inherited the titles of Shugo of Aki, Wakasa, and Tango provinces, but lost Tango in 1474. Until the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the Takeda were Shugo of the provinces of Kai (since Yoritomo), {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|WD=Q965029|lt=Aki|1=Aki Province}} (since 1221), and {{ill|Wakasa Province|en|Wakasa Province|WD=Q1053713|lt=Wakasa|1=Wakasa Province}} (since 1440).{{Citation needed |date=May 2020}} ===Sengoku period=== {{Campaignbox Campaigns of the Takeda}} Immediately prior to the Sengoku period, the Takeda helped to suppress the Rebellion of Uesugi Zenshū (1416–1417).{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Uesugi Zenshū, Rebellion of | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} {{ill|Uesugi Zenshū|en|Uesugi Zenshū|WD=Q7877480|lt=Uesugi Zenshū|1=Uesugi Zenshū}} (d. 1417) was the ''{{ill|Kanrei|en|Kanrei|WD=Q1202497|lt=Kanrei|1=Kanrei}}'' chief advisor to {{ill|Ashikaga Mochiuji|en|Ashikaga Mochiuji|WD=Q4805073|lt=Ashikaga Mochiuji|1=Ashikaga Mochiuji}}, an enemy of the central {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate|1=Ashikaga shogunate}} and the {{ill|Kantō kubō|en|Kantō kubō|WD=Q860777|lt=Kantō kubō|1=Kantō kubō}} governor-general of the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region|1=Kantō region}}. Mochiuji, lord of the [[Uesugi clan]], made a reprisal against the Takeda clan in 1415. This reprisal began a rivalry between the [[Uesugi clan|Uesugi]] and Takeda clans which would last roughly 150 years until the destruction of the Takeda clan at the end of the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Uesugi family | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} While this rivalry existed, the {{ill|Takeda clan (Aki)|en|Takeda clan (Aki)|WD=Q2026427|lt=Takeda|1=Takeda clan (Aki)}} and the [[Uesugi clan|Uesugi]] still had a huge amount of respect for one another. ===Takeda Shingen=== [[File:Komoro castle04s3872.jpg|220px|right|thumb|Komoro Castle, a Takeda clan's castle in Shinano province]] {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Harunobu|1=Takeda Shingen}} (1521 – 1573) succeeded his father Nobutora in 1540 and became ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' lord of {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}} in present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|WD=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}}. In this period the Takeda began to quickly expand from their base in Kai Province. In 1559, Harunobu changed his name to the better-known Takeda Shingen. He faced the {{ill|Later Hōjō clan|en|Later Hōjō clan|WD=Q431928|lt=Hōjō clan|1=Later Hōjō clan}} a number of times, and most of his expansion was to the north, where he fought his most famous battles against {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|en|Uesugi Kenshin|WD=Q311080|lt=Uesugi Kenshin|1=Uesugi Kenshin}}. This series of regional skirmishes is known as the {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battles of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}}. The battles began in 1553, and the best known and severest among them was fought on September 10, 1561.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Takeda Shingen | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} Shingen is famous for his tactical genius, and innovations, though some historians have argued that his tactics were not particularly impressive nor revolutionary. Nevertheless, Shingen is perhaps most famous for his use of the {{ill|Cavalry|en|Cavalry|WD=Q47315|lt=Cavalry|1=Cavalry}} charge at the {{ill|Battle of Mikatagahara|en|Battle of Mikatagahara|WD=Q690464|lt=Battle of Mikatagahara|1=Battle of Mikatagahara}}. The strength of Shingen's new tactic became so famous that the Takeda army came to be known as the ''Kiba Gundan'' (騎馬軍団), or 'mounted army'. Up until the mid-16th century and Shingen's rise to power, mounted ''samurai'' were primarily archers. There was already a trend at this time towards larger {{ill|infantry|en|infantry|WD=Q29171|lt=infantry|1=Infantry}}-based armies, including a large number of foot archers. In order to defeat these missile troops, Shingen transformed his ''samurai'' from {{ill|Archery|en|Archery|WD=Q108429|lt=archer|1=Archery}}s to {{ill|lancer|en|lancer|WD=Q1045848|lt=lancer|1=Lancer}}s. ===Decline of the Takeda clan=== [[File:Koshukin.jpg|thumb|Gold coin of the Takeda clan of Kai (also called {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kōshū|1=Kai Province}} (甲州金)) in the 16th century, an early example of {{ill|Japanese currency|en|Japanese currency|WD=Q6158487|lt=Japanese currency|1=Japanese currency}} ]] Shingen died on May 13, 1573, at age 53 from illness.{{cite book | last = E. Deal | first = William | authorlink = | title = Handbook to Life in Medieval and Early Modern Japan | publisher = Oxford University Press US | year = 2007 | location = | pages = 44–45 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=DY0XiflmVIAC | isbn = 978-0-19-533126-4}} His son [[Takeda Katsuyori]] (1546–1582) effectively succeeded Shingen though the nominal head of the family was his grandson Takeda Nobukatsu; Katsuyori continued Shingen's aggressive expansion plan south and westward and was initially successful, briefly achieving the largest extent of Takeda rule. However, he was defeated in the {{ill|Battle of Nagashino|en|Battle of Nagashino|WD=Q428369|lt=Battle of Nagashino|1=Battle of Nagashino}} in 1575 by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|WD=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga|1=Oda Nobunaga}} and {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}. After Nagashino, the Takeda clan fell into sharp decline as it had lost many of its most notable samurai during the battle. Katsuyori's position within the clan also became precarious (as he did not fully inherit the clan leadership position); in 1582, two of his relatives defected to the Oda/Tokugawa alliance and Nobunaga succeeded in destroying the Takeda clan shortly thereafter. The campaign saw most of the Takeda followers simply abandoning Katsuyori and the other Takeda family members to their fate. The clan was effectively eliminated, although descendants of the Takeda clan would take prominent positions in the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], established in 1603. ==Modern period== Takeda is also a fairly common family name in modern Japan, though it is unlikely that everyone with the Takeda name is descended from this noble house (several divisions of the family have the Takeda name). In fact, most of the real descendants of the Takeda had a different name when they created a cadet branch. It is also acknowledged that members of the clan married into other Japanese families. During the [[:en:Tokugawa period|Tokugawa period]], several ''daimyō'' families were direct descendants of the Takeda. In 1868, these ''daimyō'' families were : * The {{ill|Matsumae clan|en|Matsumae clan|WD=Q1061883|lt=Matsumae|1=Matsumae clan}}, descendants of Takeda Nobuhiro (1431-1494), son of Takeda Nobukata (1420-1471) of the Aki Takeda. They were ''daimyō'' of Matsumae, the only feudal fief (''[[:en:Han (country subdivision)|han]]'') of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]]. * The {{ill|Nanbu clan|en|Nanbu clan|WD=Q2975330|lt=Nanbu|1=Nanbu clan}}, descendants of Takeda Mitsuyuki (1165-1236), grandson of Takeda Kiyomitsu (1110-1168), established himself at Nambu ({{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}}) and took that name. The Nambu were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Morioka Domain|en|Morioka Domain|WD=Q908854|lt=Morioka|1=Morioka Domain}}, of {{ill|Shichinohe Domain|en|Shichinohe Domain|WD=Q7884520|lt=Shichinohe|1=Shichinohe Domain}} and {{ill|Hachinohe Domain|en|Hachinohe Domain|WD=Q7884927|lt=Hachinohe|1=Hachinohe Domain}} ({{ill|Mutsu Province|en|Mutsu Province|WD=Q907389|lt=Mutsu Province|1=Mutsu Province}}). * The {{ill|Yanagisawa clan|en|Yanagisawa clan|WD=Q11534410|lt=Yanagisawa|1=Yanagisawa clan}}, descendants of Takeda Nobunaga, a grandson of Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128-1186), were ''daimyō'' of Kōriyama ({{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}}), of {{ill|Kurokawa Domain|en|Kurokawa Domain|WD=Q849395|lt=Kurokawa|1=Kurokawa Domain}} and {{ill|Mikkaichi Domain|en|Mikkaichi Domain|WD=Q849472|lt=Mikkaichi|1=Mikkaichi Domain}} ({{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}}). * The {{ill|Yonekura clan|en|Yonekura clan|WD=Q2975397|lt=Yonekura|1=Yonekura clan}}, descendants of Takeda Kiyomitsu, settled at Koiwasuji Yonekura and took the name Yonekura. They were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Mutsuura Domain|en|Mutsuura Domain|WD=Q3034502|lt=Mutsuura Domain|1=Mutsuura Domain}} (Musashi province) * The Gotō, descendants of Takeda Nobuhiro, were ''daimyō'' of Gotō (the {{ill|Gotō Islands|en|Gotō Islands|WD=Q1333790|lt=Gotō Islands|1=Gotō Islands}} in {{ill|Hizen Province|en|Hizen Province|WD=Q906926|lt=Hizen Province|1=Hizen Province}}). * The {{ill|Ogasawara clan|en|Ogasawara clan|WD=Q2975340|lt=Ogasawara|1=Ogasawara clan}} are also a cadet branch of the Takeda, by Takeda Nagakiyo (1162–1242), grandson of Takeda Kiyomitsu (1110-1168), and the first to take the name of Ogasawara. His descendants were ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' (governors) of {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|WD=Q289250|lt=Shinano|1=Shinano Province}} and {{ill|Hida Province|en|Hida Province|WD=Q1056535|lt=Hida Province|1=Hida Province}}s, and during the 16th century were at war with their Takeda cousins. In 1868, they were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Kokura Domain|en|Kokura Domain|WD=Q1140943|lt=Kokura|1=Kokura Domain}}, of Chikuza ({{ill|Buzen Province|en|Buzen Province|WD=Q1047134|lt=Buzen Province|1=Buzen Province}}), of Ashi ({{ill|Harima Province|en|Harima Province|WD=Q1047523|lt=Harima Province|1=Harima Province}}), of {{ill|Karatsu Domain|en|Karatsu Domain|WD=Q743925|lt=Karatsu|1=Karatsu Domain}} (Hizen Province), and of {{ill|Echizen-Katsuyama Domain|en|Echizen-Katsuyama Domain|WD=Q10863286|lt=Katsuyama|1=Echizen-Katsuyama Domain}} (Echizen Province). In 1868, two branches named Takeda were also Ranked among the ''{{ill|Kōke|en|Kōke|WD=Q11669183|lt=Kōke|1=Kōke}}'' (the High Families). This title was given to descendants of great dispossessed ''[[daimyo]]'' families of the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}} to {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}} such as the Takeda, the {{ill|Kyōgoku clan|en|Kyōgoku clan|WD=Q2975299|lt=Kyōgoku|1=Kyōgoku clan}}, the {{ill|Rokkaku clan|en|Rokkaku clan|WD=Q2975342|lt=Rokkaku|1=Rokkaku clan}}, the {{ill|Ōtomo clan|en|Ōtomo clan|WD=Q1096662|lt=Ōtomo|1=Ōtomo clan}}, the [[Toki clan|Toki]], the {{ill|Isshiki clan|en|Isshiki clan|WD=Q11353128|lt=Isshiki|1=Isshiki clan}} and the [[Hatakeyama clan|Hatakeyama]] clans. They received a pension from the shogunate and had privileged missions confided to them. == Cadet branches == [[File:Satoukanayamajou01.JPG|left|thumb|Site of Kanayama Castle (Hiroshima Prefecture), a huge mountain castle surrounded by 50 {{ill|Kuruwa|en|Kuruwa|WD=Q6447542|lt=Kuruwa|1=Kuruwa}} (castle defense walls), on top of the 411m of Mt Takeda, built at the end of the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, the seat of the Aki Takeda]] [[File:Mariyatsu-Castle Senjyojiki.JPG|left|thumb|Site of Mariyatsu Castle ([[:en:Kisarazu, Chiba|Kisarazu]], {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|WD=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}), Koguchi (entrance of castle), the seat of the Kazusa Takeda]] Three major cadet branches of the Takeda clan were established across Japan, along with several smaller branches. Due to the establishment of these cadet branches, the main Takeda clan in Kai Province is also referred to as the Kai Takeda clan. ===Aki Takeda=== The [[:en:Aki Takeda clan|Aki Takeda clan]], established in {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|WD=Q965029|lt=Aki Province|1=Aki Province}} in the present-day western part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}}. Takeda Nobumitsu (1162–1248), Shugo of Kai, received the governorship of Aki province in 1221. [[Takeda Nobutake]] († 1362) was the last Takeda ''Shugo'' of the two provinces of Kai and Aki. His elder son Nobunari received Kai and the younger Ujinobu received Aki province. ===Wakasa Takeda=== The Aki Takeda was granted the governorship of Wakasa province in 1440. The Wakasa Takeda clan was established in {{ill|Wakasa Province|en|Wakasa Province|WD=Q1053713|lt=Wakasa Province|1=Wakasa Province}} in present-day southern {{ill|Fukui Prefecture|en|Fukui Prefecture|WD=Q133879|lt=Fukui Prefecture|1=Fukui Prefecture}}, and separates from Aki province in 1500, when Takeda Motonobu (1461-1521) ruled Wakasa, while his uncle Takeda Mototsuna (1441-1505) ruled Aki. The Wakasa Takeda were known for their patronage of the arts and developing the Takeda school of military etiquette. ===Kazusa Takeda=== The Kazusa Takeda clan, established at the beginning of the Sengoku period in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en|Kazusa Province|WD=Q1055394|lt=Kazusa Province|1=Kazusa Province}} in the present-day central area of {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|WD=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}. Along with the {{ill|Satomi clan|en|Satomi clan|WD=Q2975367|lt=Satomi clan|1=Satomi clan}} of {{ill|Awa Province (Chiba)|en|Awa Province (Chiba)|WD=Q1053044|lt=Awa Province|1=Awa Province (Chiba)}} in the southern part of present-day Chiba Prefecture the two clans replaced the dominance of the [[Chiba clan]] in the region. The Kazusa Takeda is also known as the Mariyatsu Takeda, a reference to their base of power, Mariyatsu Castle. ==Clan literature== The ''Kōshū Hatto'', composed at some point in the 15th century, is the code of law of the Takeda family,{{Cite book|last=Ikegami|first=Eiko|title=The Taming of the Samurai: Honorific Individualism and the Making of Modern Japan|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=1997|isbn=978-0-674-25466-4|language=en}} while the ''{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|en|Kōyō Gunkan|WD=Q586111|lt=Kōyō Gunkan|1=Kōyō Gunkan}}'', composed largely by {{ill|Kōsaka Masanobu|en|Kōsaka Masanobu|WD=Q2477835|lt=Kōsaka Masanobu|1=Kōsaka Masanobu}} in the mid-16th century, is an {{ill|Epic poetry|en|Epic poetry|WD=Q37484|lt=epic poem|1=Epic poetry}} recording the family's history and Shingen's innovations in military tactics. ==Notable figures of the Takeda clan== Among the notable members of the Takeda clan was {{ill|Takeda Nobushige|en|Takeda Nobushige|WD=Q1350640|lt=Takeda Nobushige|1=Takeda Nobushige}}, who wrote the ''Kyujukyu Kakun'', which introduced the 99 rules for the clan members.{{Cite book|last=Ekholm|first=Thomas|title=Japans historia|last2=Ottosson|first2=Ingemar|publisher=Svenska Historiska Media Förlag AB|year=2015|isbn=978-91-87263-02-6|language=sv}} {{ill|Nobumitsu|en|Nobumitsu|WD=Q7046192|lt=Takeda Nobumitsu|1=Nobumitsu}}, who was a noted warrior under the Hojo shikken of Kamakura, became a monk and founded the Takeda family of Kai.{{Cite book|last=Frederic|first=Louis|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=2002|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|location=Cambridge, MA|pages=939}} Another important figure was Minamoto no Yoshimitsu, who developed the ''{{ill|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|en|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|WD=Q1500342|lt=Daito-ryu Aikijujutsu|1=Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu}}/[[Takeda Ryu Nakamura Ha#Takeda Ryu history|Takeda-ryu]]''.{{Cite book|last=Shaw|first=Scott|title=Hapkido: Korean Art of Self-Defense|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4629-0344-3|location=North Clarendon, VT|language=en}} Other noted members include {{ill|Takeda Nobuyoshi|en|Takeda Nobuyoshi|WD=Q1133267|lt=Nobuyoshi|1=Takeda Nobuyoshi}}, {{ill|Takeda Nobutora|en|Takeda Nobutora|WD=Q1192628|lt=Nobutora|1=Takeda Nobutora}}, {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Harunobu (Shingen)|1=Takeda Shingen}}, [[Takeda Katsuyori|Katsuyori]], {{ill|Matsuhime|en|Matsuhime|WD=Q10368377|lt=Matsuhime|1=Matsuhime}} === Important members === *{{ill|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|en|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|WD=Q7392303|lt=Takeda Nobuyoshi|1=Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)}} (1128–86) Founder of the Takeda clan *{{ill|Takeda Nobutora|en|Takeda Nobutora|WD=Q1192628|lt=Takeda Nobutora|1=Takeda Nobutora}} – Shingen's father *{{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen|1=Takeda Shingen}} – one of Japan's most famous warlords, Shingen expanded his domains greatly and became one of the major powers in the country for a time. *[[Takeda Katsuyori]] – Shingen's son, Katsuyori commanded his father's armies after his death, and saw the fall of the Takeda family. *{{ill|Matsuhime|en|Matsuhime|WD=Q10368377|lt=Matsuhime|1=Matsuhime}} – Shingen's daughter *{{ill|Takeda Nobushige|en|Takeda Nobushige|WD=Q1350640|lt=Takeda Nobushige|1=Takeda Nobushige}} – Shingen's younger brother, who held their father's favor to be heir of the clan, continued to support his older brother throughout his life, he also wrote the ''Kyūjūkyū Kakun'', a set of 99 short rules for Takeda house members. *{{ill|Takeda Sōkaku|en|Takeda Sōkaku|WD=Q503880|lt=Takeda Sōkaku|1=Takeda Sōkaku}} (1859–1943) was the restorer of the {{ill|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|en|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|WD=Q1500342|lt=Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|1=Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu}} school of [[:en:Jūjutsu|Jūjutsu]], and the first to teach the art outside of the Takeda family.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Nihon Jinmei Daijiten (日本人名大辞典) | title = Takeda Sōkaku (武田惣角) | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-04-10 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | language = Japanese | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} == Crests == *Four diamonds (pictured) *Four diamonds surrounded by a solid ring *Two cranes bowing their heads together *A centipede *Hanabishi (three vertical flowers) *{{ill|Fūrinkazan|en|Fūrinkazan|WD=Q1101037|lt=Fūrinkazan|1=Fūrinkazan}} (a battle standard with the writing: "風林火山", which literally means: "Wind, Forest, Fire, Mountain".) *The Tai (大) character ==Popular culture== Takeda is a playable faction in ''{{ill|Shogun: Total War|en|Shogun: Total War|WD=Q528310|lt=Shogun: Total War|1=Shogun: Total War}}'' and ''[[:en:Shogun 2|Shogun 2]]''. Takeda is a playable nation in ''{{ill|Europa Universalis IV|en|Europa Universalis IV|WD=Q2625075|lt=Europa Universalis IV|1=Europa Universalis IV}}''. The Takeda clan in feudal Japan is in the manga and the anime of ''{{ill|Inuyasha|en|Inuyasha|WD=Q182056|lt=Inuyasha|1=Inuyasha}}''. Takeda Shingen and his peasant {{ill|Doppelgänger|en|Doppelgänger|WD=Q461363|lt=Doppelgänger|1=Doppelgänger}} are the main subjects of ''{{ill|Kagemusha|en|Kagemusha|WD=Q854990|lt=Kagemusha|1=Kagemusha}}'', directed by {{ill|Akira Kurosawa|en|Akira Kurosawa|WD=Q8006|lt=Akira Kurosawa|1=Akira Kurosawa}}. The character Miku Nakano from the anime and manga series ''{{ill|The Quintessential Quintuplets|en|The Quintessential Quintuplets|WD=Q38277250|lt=The Quintessential Quintuplets|1=The Quintessential Quintuplets}}'' is shown to have an obsession with Takeda Shingen. The Soldier in ''{{ill|Team Fortress 2|en|Team Fortress 2|WD=Q382108|lt=Team Fortress 2|1=Team Fortress 2}}'' has a weapon called the Concheror that includes the Takeda clan's Kamon.{{cite web|url=https://wiki.teamfortress.com/wiki/Concheror|title=Conceror - Team Fortress 2 wiki|author=Valve|access-date=August 16, 2024}} ==References== ==Further reading== * Sansom, George (1961). ''A History of Japan: 1334–1615''. Stanford: Stanford University Press. * Turnbull, Stephen (1998). ''The Samurai Sourcebook''. London: Cassell & Co. * Turnbull, Stephen (2002). ''War in Japan 1467–1615''. {{ill|Akiyama clan|en|Akiyama clan|WD=Q2975207|lt=Akiyama clan|1=Akiyama clan}} }} The '''{{nihongo|Takeda Clan|武田氏|Takeda-shi}}''' was a Japanese {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} clan active from the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} until the late 16th century. The clan was historically based in {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}} in present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|WD=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}}.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Kokushi Daijiten (国史大辞典) | title = Takeda-shi (武田氏) | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-09 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | language = Japanese | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }}{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Takeda family | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} The clan reached its greatest influence under the rule of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen|1=Takeda Shingen}}, one of the most famous rulers of the period. ==History== ===Origin=== [[File:Yōshū Chikanobu Shiragi Saburo and Tokiaki.jpg|thumb|right|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu was famous in horsemanship and archery, here playing the musical instrument {{ill|Shō (instrument)|en|Shō (instrument)|WD=Q1975355|lt=shō|1=Shō (instrument)}}]] The Takeda are descendants of the {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa|1=Emperor Seiwa}} (858–876), the 56th Emperor of Japan, and are a branch of the [[Minamoto clan]] ({{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji|1=Seiwa Genji}}), by {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|WD=Q3083118|lt=Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|1=Minamoto no Yoshimitsu}} (1056–1127), son of the ''[[:en:Chinjufu-shōgun|Chinjufu-shōgun]]'' [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988-1075), and brother to the famous {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie|1=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} (1039–1106).{{Cite book|last=Hubbard|first=Ben|title=Samurai Warriors|publisher=Cavendish Square Publishing, LLC|year=2017|isbn=978-1-5026-2459-8|location=New York, NY|pages=64}}{{Cite book|last=Shaw|first=Scott|title=Hapkido: Korean Art of Self-Defense|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4629-0344-3|language=en}} {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|en|Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|WD=Q6863154|lt=Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|1=Minamoto no Yoshikiyo}} (1075–1149), son of Yoshimitsu, was the first to take the name of Takeda, which he took when his father granted him Takeda domain in {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|WD=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi Province|1=Hitachi Province}}; thereafter, he was known as Takeda Yoshikiyo. ===Kamakura to early Azuchi–Momoyama periods=== In the 12th century, at the end of the Heian period, the Takeda family-controlled {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}}. Along with a number of other families, they supported their cousin [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] against the [[Taira clan|Taira]] clan in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War|1=Genpei War}} (1180–85). When Yoritomo was first defeated at Ishibashiyama (1181), {{ill|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|en|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|WD=Q7392303|lt=Takeda Nobuyoshi|1=Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)}} (1128–86) was applied for help, and the Takeda sent an army of 25,000 soldiers to support Yoritomo. Takeda Nobumitsu (1162–1248), son of Nobuyoshi, fought against the Taira, against {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|en|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|WD=Q1139202|lt=Kiso Yoshinaka|1=Minamoto no Yoshinaka}} (1184), distinguished himself in the [[:en:Battle of Ichinotani|Battle of Ichinotani]] (1184), and was appointed ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' (Governor) of Kai province. He also fought against the {{ill|Northern Fujiwara|en|Northern Fujiwara|WD=Q1050942|lt=Northern Fujiwara|1=Northern Fujiwara}} (1189) and against {{ill|Wada Yoshimori|en|Wada Yoshimori|WD=Q3564968|lt=Wada Yoshimori|1=Wada Yoshimori}} (1213). During the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}}, he helped the {{ill|Hōjō clan|en|Hōjō clan|WD=Q834364|lt=Hōjō|1=Hōjō clan}}, and led 50,000 soldiers as 'Daishōgun of the Tosando' , and in reward received the governorship of Aki province (1221). Takeda Nobuhide (1413–40), eldest son of the Takeda Nobushige (1390–1465), Shugo of Aki, helped the 6th shogun {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshinori|en|Ashikaga Yoshinori|WD=Q239170|lt=Ashikaga Yoshinori|1=Ashikaga Yoshinori}} (1394–1441) against the revolt of Isshiki Yoshitsura and was granted the governorship of Wakasa province (1440). Takeda Nobukata (1420–71) inherited the titles of Shugo of Wakasa from his brother Nobuhide, and that of Shugo of Aki from his father Nobushige. During the {{ill|Ōnin War|en|Ōnin War|WD=Q385676|lt=Ōnin War|1=Ōnin War}} (1467–77) he occupied Tango province that belonged to Isshiki Yoshinao and received the governorship of Tango province (1469). His brother Takeda Kuninobu (1437–90) inherited the titles of Shugo of Aki, Wakasa, and Tango provinces, but lost Tango in 1474. Until the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the Takeda were Shugo of the provinces of Kai (since Yoritomo), {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|WD=Q965029|lt=Aki|1=Aki Province}} (since 1221), and {{ill|Wakasa Province|en|Wakasa Province|WD=Q1053713|lt=Wakasa|1=Wakasa Province}} (since 1440).{{Citation needed |date=May 2020}} ===Sengoku period=== {{Campaignbox Campaigns of the Takeda}} Immediately prior to the Sengoku period, the Takeda helped to suppress the Rebellion of Uesugi Zenshū (1416–1417).{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Uesugi Zenshū, Rebellion of | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} {{ill|Uesugi Zenshū|en|Uesugi Zenshū|WD=Q7877480|lt=Uesugi Zenshū|1=Uesugi Zenshū}} (d. 1417) was the ''{{ill|Kanrei|en|Kanrei|WD=Q1202497|lt=Kanrei|1=Kanrei}}'' chief advisor to {{ill|Ashikaga Mochiuji|en|Ashikaga Mochiuji|WD=Q4805073|lt=Ashikaga Mochiuji|1=Ashikaga Mochiuji}}, an enemy of the central {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate|1=Ashikaga shogunate}} and the {{ill|Kantō kubō|en|Kantō kubō|WD=Q860777|lt=Kantō kubō|1=Kantō kubō}} governor-general of the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region|1=Kantō region}}. Mochiuji, lord of the [[Uesugi clan]], made a reprisal against the Takeda clan in 1415. This reprisal began a rivalry between the [[Uesugi clan|Uesugi]] and Takeda clans which would last roughly 150 years until the destruction of the Takeda clan at the end of the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Uesugi family | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} While this rivalry existed, the {{ill|Takeda clan (Aki)|en|Takeda clan (Aki)|WD=Q2026427|lt=Takeda|1=Takeda clan (Aki)}} and the [[Uesugi clan|Uesugi]] still had a huge amount of respect for one another. ===Takeda Shingen=== [[File:Komoro castle04s3872.jpg|220px|right|thumb|Komoro Castle, a Takeda clan's castle in Shinano province]] {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Harunobu|1=Takeda Shingen}} (1521 – 1573) succeeded his father Nobutora in 1540 and became ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' lord of {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}} in present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|WD=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}}. In this period the Takeda began to quickly expand from their base in Kai Province. In 1559, Harunobu changed his name to the better-known Takeda Shingen. He faced the {{ill|Later Hōjō clan|en|Later Hōjō clan|WD=Q431928|lt=Hōjō clan|1=Later Hōjō clan}} a number of times, and most of his expansion was to the north, where he fought his most famous battles against {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|en|Uesugi Kenshin|WD=Q311080|lt=Uesugi Kenshin|1=Uesugi Kenshin}}. This series of regional skirmishes is known as the {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battles of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}}. The battles began in 1553, and the best known and severest among them was fought on September 10, 1561.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Takeda Shingen | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} Shingen is famous for his tactical genius, and innovations, though some historians have argued that his tactics were not particularly impressive nor revolutionary. Nevertheless, Shingen is perhaps most famous for his use of the {{ill|Cavalry|en|Cavalry|WD=Q47315|lt=Cavalry|1=Cavalry}} charge at the {{ill|Battle of Mikatagahara|en|Battle of Mikatagahara|WD=Q690464|lt=Battle of Mikatagahara|1=Battle of Mikatagahara}}. The strength of Shingen's new tactic became so famous that the Takeda army came to be known as the ''Kiba Gundan'' (騎馬軍団), or 'mounted army'. Up until the mid-16th century and Shingen's rise to power, mounted ''samurai'' were primarily archers. There was already a trend at this time towards larger {{ill|infantry|en|infantry|WD=Q29171|lt=infantry|1=Infantry}}-based armies, including a large number of foot archers. In order to defeat these missile troops, Shingen transformed his ''samurai'' from {{ill|Archery|en|Archery|WD=Q108429|lt=archer|1=Archery}}s to {{ill|lancer|en|lancer|WD=Q1045848|lt=lancer|1=Lancer}}s. ===Decline of the Takeda clan=== [[File:Koshukin.jpg|thumb|Gold coin of the Takeda clan of Kai (also called {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kōshū|1=Kai Province}} (甲州金)) in the 16th century, an early example of {{ill|Japanese currency|en|Japanese currency|WD=Q6158487|lt=Japanese currency|1=Japanese currency}} ]] Shingen died on May 13, 1573, at age 53 from illness.{{cite book | last = E. Deal | first = William | authorlink = | title = Handbook to Life in Medieval and Early Modern Japan | publisher = Oxford University Press US | year = 2007 | location = | pages = 44–45 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=DY0XiflmVIAC | isbn = 978-0-19-533126-4}} His son [[Takeda Katsuyori]] (1546–1582) effectively succeeded Shingen though the nominal head of the family was his grandson Takeda Nobukatsu; Katsuyori continued Shingen's aggressive expansion plan south and westward and was initially successful, briefly achieving the largest extent of Takeda rule. However, he was defeated in the {{ill|Battle of Nagashino|en|Battle of Nagashino|WD=Q428369|lt=Battle of Nagashino|1=Battle of Nagashino}} in 1575 by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|WD=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga|1=Oda Nobunaga}} and {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}. After Nagashino, the Takeda clan fell into sharp decline as it had lost many of its most notable samurai during the battle. Katsuyori's position within the clan also became precarious (as he did not fully inherit the clan leadership position); in 1582, two of his relatives defected to the Oda/Tokugawa alliance and Nobunaga succeeded in destroying the Takeda clan shortly thereafter. The campaign saw most of the Takeda followers simply abandoning Katsuyori and the other Takeda family members to their fate. The clan was effectively eliminated, although descendants of the Takeda clan would take prominent positions in the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], established in 1603. ==Modern period== Takeda is also a fairly common family name in modern Japan, though it is unlikely that everyone with the Takeda name is descended from this noble house (several divisions of the family have the Takeda name). In fact, most of the real descendants of the Takeda had a different name when they created a cadet branch. It is also acknowledged that members of the clan married into other Japanese families. During the [[:en:Tokugawa period|Tokugawa period]], several ''daimyō'' families were direct descendants of the Takeda. In 1868, these ''daimyō'' families were : * The {{ill|Matsumae clan|en|Matsumae clan|WD=Q1061883|lt=Matsumae|1=Matsumae clan}}, descendants of Takeda Nobuhiro (1431-1494), son of Takeda Nobukata (1420-1471) of the Aki Takeda. They were ''daimyō'' of Matsumae, the only feudal fief (''[[:en:Han (country subdivision)|han]]'') of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]]. * The {{ill|Nanbu clan|en|Nanbu clan|WD=Q2975330|lt=Nanbu|1=Nanbu clan}}, descendants of Takeda Mitsuyuki (1165-1236), grandson of Takeda Kiyomitsu (1110-1168), established himself at Nambu ({{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}}) and took that name. The Nambu were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Morioka Domain|en|Morioka Domain|WD=Q908854|lt=Morioka|1=Morioka Domain}}, of {{ill|Shichinohe Domain|en|Shichinohe Domain|WD=Q7884520|lt=Shichinohe|1=Shichinohe Domain}} and {{ill|Hachinohe Domain|en|Hachinohe Domain|WD=Q7884927|lt=Hachinohe|1=Hachinohe Domain}} ({{ill|Mutsu Province|en|Mutsu Province|WD=Q907389|lt=Mutsu Province|1=Mutsu Province}}). * The {{ill|Yanagisawa clan|en|Yanagisawa clan|WD=Q11534410|lt=Yanagisawa|1=Yanagisawa clan}}, descendants of Takeda Nobunaga, a grandson of Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128-1186), were ''daimyō'' of Kōriyama ({{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}}), of {{ill|Kurokawa Domain|en|Kurokawa Domain|WD=Q849395|lt=Kurokawa|1=Kurokawa Domain}} and {{ill|Mikkaichi Domain|en|Mikkaichi Domain|WD=Q849472|lt=Mikkaichi|1=Mikkaichi Domain}} ({{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}}). * The {{ill|Yonekura clan|en|Yonekura clan|WD=Q2975397|lt=Yonekura|1=Yonekura clan}}, descendants of Takeda Kiyomitsu, settled at Koiwasuji Yonekura and took the name Yonekura. They were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Mutsuura Domain|en|Mutsuura Domain|WD=Q3034502|lt=Mutsuura Domain|1=Mutsuura Domain}} (Musashi province) * The Gotō, descendants of Takeda Nobuhiro, were ''daimyō'' of Gotō (the {{ill|Gotō Islands|en|Gotō Islands|WD=Q1333790|lt=Gotō Islands|1=Gotō Islands}} in {{ill|Hizen Province|en|Hizen Province|WD=Q906926|lt=Hizen Province|1=Hizen Province}}). * The {{ill|Ogasawara clan|en|Ogasawara clan|WD=Q2975340|lt=Ogasawara|1=Ogasawara clan}} are also a cadet branch of the Takeda, by Takeda Nagakiyo (1162–1242), grandson of Takeda Kiyomitsu (1110-1168), and the first to take the name of Ogasawara. His descendants were ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' (governors) of {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|WD=Q289250|lt=Shinano|1=Shinano Province}} and {{ill|Hida Province|en|Hida Province|WD=Q1056535|lt=Hida Province|1=Hida Province}}s, and during the 16th century were at war with their Takeda cousins. In 1868, they were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Kokura Domain|en|Kokura Domain|WD=Q1140943|lt=Kokura|1=Kokura Domain}}, of Chikuza ({{ill|Buzen Province|en|Buzen Province|WD=Q1047134|lt=Buzen Province|1=Buzen Province}}), of Ashi ({{ill|Harima Province|en|Harima Province|WD=Q1047523|lt=Harima Province|1=Harima Province}}), of {{ill|Karatsu Domain|en|Karatsu Domain|WD=Q743925|lt=Karatsu|1=Karatsu Domain}} (Hizen Province), and of {{ill|Echizen-Katsuyama Domain|en|Echizen-Katsuyama Domain|WD=Q10863286|lt=Katsuyama|1=Echizen-Katsuyama Domain}} (Echizen Province). In 1868, two branches named Takeda were also Ranked among the ''{{ill|Kōke|en|Kōke|WD=Q11669183|lt=Kōke|1=Kōke}}'' (the High Families). This title was given to descendants of great dispossessed ''[[daimyo]]'' families of the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}} to {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}} such as the Takeda, the {{ill|Kyōgoku clan|en|Kyōgoku clan|WD=Q2975299|lt=Kyōgoku|1=Kyōgoku clan}}, the {{ill|Rokkaku clan|en|Rokkaku clan|WD=Q2975342|lt=Rokkaku|1=Rokkaku clan}}, the {{ill|Ōtomo clan|en|Ōtomo clan|WD=Q1096662|lt=Ōtomo|1=Ōtomo clan}}, the [[Toki clan|Toki]], the {{ill|Isshiki clan|en|Isshiki clan|WD=Q11353128|lt=Isshiki|1=Isshiki clan}} and the [[Hatakeyama clan|Hatakeyama]] clans. They received a pension from the shogunate and had privileged missions confided to them. == Cadet branches == [[File:Satoukanayamajou01.JPG|left|thumb|Site of Kanayama Castle (Hiroshima Prefecture), a huge mountain castle surrounded by 50 {{ill|Kuruwa|en|Kuruwa|WD=Q6447542|lt=Kuruwa|1=Kuruwa}} (castle defense walls), on top of the 411m of Mt Takeda, built at the end of the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, the seat of the Aki Takeda]] [[File:Mariyatsu-Castle Senjyojiki.JPG|left|thumb|Site of Mariyatsu Castle ([[:en:Kisarazu, Chiba|Kisarazu]], {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|WD=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}), Koguchi (entrance of castle), the seat of the Kazusa Takeda]] Three major cadet branches of the Takeda clan were established across Japan, along with several smaller branches. Due to the establishment of these cadet branches, the main Takeda clan in Kai Province is also referred to as the Kai Takeda clan. ===Aki Takeda=== The [[:en:Aki Takeda clan|Aki Takeda clan]], established in {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|WD=Q965029|lt=Aki Province|1=Aki Province}} in the present-day western part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}}. Takeda Nobumitsu (1162–1248), Shugo of Kai, received the governorship of Aki province in 1221. [[Takeda Nobutake]] († 1362) was the last Takeda ''Shugo'' of the two provinces of Kai and Aki. His elder son Nobunari received Kai and the younger Ujinobu received Aki province. ===Wakasa Takeda=== The Aki Takeda was granted the governorship of Wakasa province in 1440. The Wakasa Takeda clan was established in {{ill|Wakasa Province|en|Wakasa Province|WD=Q1053713|lt=Wakasa Province|1=Wakasa Province}} in present-day southern {{ill|Fukui Prefecture|en|Fukui Prefecture|WD=Q133879|lt=Fukui Prefecture|1=Fukui Prefecture}}, and separates from Aki province in 1500, when Takeda Motonobu (1461-1521) ruled Wakasa, while his uncle Takeda Mototsuna (1441-1505) ruled Aki. The Wakasa Takeda were known for their patronage of the arts and developing the Takeda school of military etiquette. ===Kazusa Takeda=== The Kazusa Takeda clan, established at the beginning of the Sengoku period in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en|Kazusa Province|WD=Q1055394|lt=Kazusa Province|1=Kazusa Province}} in the present-day central area of {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|WD=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}. Along with the {{ill|Satomi clan|en|Satomi clan|WD=Q2975367|lt=Satomi clan|1=Satomi clan}} of {{ill|Awa Province (Chiba)|en|Awa Province (Chiba)|WD=Q1053044|lt=Awa Province|1=Awa Province (Chiba)}} in the southern part of present-day Chiba Prefecture the two clans replaced the dominance of the [[Chiba clan]] in the region. The Kazusa Takeda is also known as the Mariyatsu Takeda, a reference to their base of power, Mariyatsu Castle. ==Clan literature== The ''Kōshū Hatto'', composed at some point in the 15th century, is the code of law of the Takeda family,{{Cite book|last=Ikegami|first=Eiko|title=The Taming of the Samurai: Honorific Individualism and the Making of Modern Japan|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=1997|isbn=978-0-674-25466-4|language=en}} while the ''{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|en|Kōyō Gunkan|WD=Q586111|lt=Kōyō Gunkan|1=Kōyō Gunkan}}'', composed largely by {{ill|Kōsaka Masanobu|en|Kōsaka Masanobu|WD=Q2477835|lt=Kōsaka Masanobu|1=Kōsaka Masanobu}} in the mid-16th century, is an {{ill|Epic poetry|en|Epic poetry|WD=Q37484|lt=epic poem|1=Epic poetry}} recording the family's history and Shingen's innovations in military tactics. ==Notable figures of the Takeda clan== Among the notable members of the Takeda clan was {{ill|Takeda Nobushige|en|Takeda Nobushige|WD=Q1350640|lt=Takeda Nobushige|1=Takeda Nobushige}}, who wrote the ''Kyujukyu Kakun'', which introduced the 99 rules for the clan members.{{Cite book|last=Ekholm|first=Thomas|title=Japans historia|last2=Ottosson|first2=Ingemar|publisher=Svenska Historiska Media Förlag AB|year=2015|isbn=978-91-87263-02-6|language=sv}} {{ill|Nobumitsu|en|Nobumitsu|WD=Q7046192|lt=Takeda Nobumitsu|1=Nobumitsu}}, who was a noted warrior under the Hojo shikken of Kamakura, became a monk and founded the Takeda family of Kai.{{Cite book|last=Frederic|first=Louis|title=Japan Encyclopedia|last2=Louis-Frédéric|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=2002|isbn=978-0-674-01753-5|location=Cambridge, MA|pages=939}} Another important figure was Minamoto no Yoshimitsu, who developed the ''{{ill|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|en|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|WD=Q1500342|lt=Daito-ryu Aikijujutsu|1=Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu}}/[[Takeda Ryu Nakamura Ha#Takeda Ryu history|Takeda-ryu]]''.{{Cite book|last=Shaw|first=Scott|title=Hapkido: Korean Art of Self-Defense|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4629-0344-3|location=North Clarendon, VT|language=en}} Other noted members include {{ill|Takeda Nobuyoshi|en|Takeda Nobuyoshi|WD=Q1133267|lt=Nobuyoshi|1=Takeda Nobuyoshi}}, {{ill|Takeda Nobutora|en|Takeda Nobutora|WD=Q1192628|lt=Nobutora|1=Takeda Nobutora}}, {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Harunobu (Shingen)|1=Takeda Shingen}}, [[Takeda Katsuyori|Katsuyori]], {{ill|Matsuhime|en|Matsuhime|WD=Q10368377|lt=Matsuhime|1=Matsuhime}} === Important members === *{{ill|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|en|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|WD=Q7392303|lt=Takeda Nobuyoshi|1=Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)}} (1128–86) Founder of the Takeda clan *{{ill|Takeda Nobutora|en|Takeda Nobutora|WD=Q1192628|lt=Takeda Nobutora|1=Takeda Nobutora}} – Shingen's father *{{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen|1=Takeda Shingen}} – one of Japan's most famous warlords, Shingen expanded his domains greatly and became one of the major powers in the country for a time. *[[Takeda Katsuyori]] – Shingen's son, Katsuyori commanded his father's armies after his death, and saw the fall of the Takeda family. *{{ill|Matsuhime|en|Matsuhime|WD=Q10368377|lt=Matsuhime|1=Matsuhime}} – Shingen's daughter *{{ill|Takeda Nobushige|en|Takeda Nobushige|WD=Q1350640|lt=Takeda Nobushige|1=Takeda Nobushige}} – Shingen's younger brother, who held their father's favor to be heir of the clan, continued to support his older brother throughout his life, he also wrote the ''Kyūjūkyū Kakun'', a set of 99 short rules for Takeda house members. *{{ill|Takeda Sōkaku|en|Takeda Sōkaku|WD=Q503880|lt=Takeda Sōkaku|1=Takeda Sōkaku}} (1859–1943) was the restorer of the {{ill|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|en|Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|WD=Q1500342|lt=Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu|1=Daitō-ryū Aiki-jūjutsu}} school of [[:en:Jūjutsu|Jūjutsu]], and the first to teach the art outside of the Takeda family.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Nihon Jinmei Daijiten (日本人名大辞典) | title = Takeda Sōkaku (武田惣角) | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-04-10 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | language = Japanese | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} == Crests == *Four diamonds (pictured) *Four diamonds surrounded by a solid ring *Two cranes bowing their heads together *A centipede *Hanabishi (three vertical flowers) *{{ill|Fūrinkazan|en|Fūrinkazan|WD=Q1101037|lt=Fūrinkazan|1=Fūrinkazan}} (a battle standard with the writing: "風林火山", which literally means: "Wind, Forest, Fire, Mountain".) *The Tai (大) character ==Popular culture== Takeda is a playable faction in ''{{ill|Shogun: Total War|en|Shogun: Total War|WD=Q528310|lt=Shogun: Total War|1=Shogun: Total War}}'' and ''[[:en:Shogun 2|Shogun 2]]''. Takeda is a playable nation in ''{{ill|Europa Universalis IV|en|Europa Universalis IV|WD=Q2625075|lt=Europa Universalis IV|1=Europa Universalis IV}}''. The Takeda clan in feudal Japan is in the manga and the anime of ''{{ill|Inuyasha|en|Inuyasha|WD=Q182056|lt=Inuyasha|1=Inuyasha}}''. Takeda Shingen and his peasant {{ill|Doppelgänger|en|Doppelgänger|WD=Q461363|lt=Doppelgänger|1=Doppelgänger}} are the main subjects of ''{{ill|Kagemusha|en|Kagemusha|WD=Q854990|lt=Kagemusha|1=Kagemusha}}'', directed by {{ill|Akira Kurosawa|en|Akira Kurosawa|WD=Q8006|lt=Akira Kurosawa|1=Akira Kurosawa}}. The character Miku Nakano from the anime and manga series ''{{ill|The Quintessential Quintuplets|en|The Quintessential Quintuplets|WD=Q38277250|lt=The Quintessential Quintuplets|1=The Quintessential Quintuplets}}'' is shown to have an obsession with Takeda Shingen. The Soldier in ''{{ill|Team Fortress 2|en|Team Fortress 2|WD=Q382108|lt=Team Fortress 2|1=Team Fortress 2}}'' has a weapon called the Concheror that includes the Takeda clan's Kamon.{{cite web|url=https://wiki.teamfortress.com/wiki/Concheror|title=Conceror - Team Fortress 2 wiki|author=Valve|access-date=August 16, 2024}} ==References== ==Further reading== * Sansom, George (1961). ''A History of Japan: 1334–1615''. Stanford: Stanford University Press. * Turnbull, Stephen (1998). ''The Samurai Sourcebook''. London: Cassell & Co. * Turnbull, Stephen (2002). ''War in Japan 1467–1615''. Oxford: Osprey Publishing.]] [[image:Morioka Park 1.JPG|thumb|right|Morioka Castle, the seat of the Nambu of Morioka]] [[image:140721 Kokura Castle Kitakyushu Japan01s3.jpg|thumb|220px|Kokura Castle, seat of the Ogasawara of Kokura]] [[en:Takeda clan]] [[ca:Clan Takeda]] [[cs:Klan Takeda]] [[de:Takeda (Klan)]] [[eo:Takeda (klano)]] [[es:Clan Takeda]] [[eu:Takeda klana]] [[fa:خاندان تاکدا]] [[fr:Clan Takeda]] [[glk:تاكدا كوگا]] [[hu:Takeda-ház]] [[id:Klan Takeda]] [[it:Clan Takeda]] [[ja:武田氏]] [[ko:다케다씨]] [[mk:Такеда (клан)]] [[nl:Takeda (familie)]] [[no:Takeda-klanen]] [[pl:Ród Takeda]] [[pt:Clã Takeda]] [[ru:Такэда]] [[sr:Клан Такеда]] [[th:ตระกูลทาเกดะ]] [[tr:Takeda boyu]] [[uk:Рід Такеда]] [[zh:武田氏]] {{wikidata link|Q1210114}} [[Category:Japanese clans]] [[Category:Takeda clan]] [[Category:Takeda clan| ]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]]

{{ill|Akiyama clan|en|Akiyama clan|WD=Q2975207|lt=Akiyama clan|1=Akiyama clan}} }} The '''{{nihongo|Takeda Clan|武田氏|Takeda-shi}}''' was a Japanese {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} clan active from the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} until the late 16th century. The clan was historically based in {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}} in present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|WD=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}}.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Kokushi Daijiten (国史大辞典) | title = Takeda-shi (武田氏) | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-09 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | language = Japanese | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }}{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Takeda family | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} The clan reached its greatest influence under the rule of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen|1=Takeda Shingen}}, one of the most famous rulers of the period. ==History== ===Origin=== [[File:Yōshū Chikanobu Shiragi Saburo and Tokiaki.jpg|thumb|right|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu was famous in horsemanship and archery, here playing the musical instrument {{ill|Shō (instrument)|en|Shō (instrument)|WD=Q1975355|lt=shō|1=Shō (instrument)}}]] The Takeda are descendants of the {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa|1=Emperor Seiwa}} (858–876), the 56th Emperor of Japan, and are a branch of the [[Minamoto clan]] ({{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji|1=Seiwa Genji}}), by {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|WD=Q3083118|lt=Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|1=Minamoto no Yoshimitsu}} (1056–1127), son of the ''[[:en:Chinjufu-shōgun|Chinjufu-shōgun]]'' [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] (988-1075), and brother to the famous {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie|1=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} (1039–1106).{{Cite book|last=Hubbard|first=Ben|title=Samurai Warriors|publisher=Cavendish Square Publishing, LLC|year=2017|isbn=978-1-5026-2459-8|location=New York, NY|pages=64}}{{Cite book|last=Shaw|first=Scott|title=Hapkido: Korean Art of Self-Defense|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4629-0344-3|language=en}} {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|en|Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|WD=Q6863154|lt=Minamoto no Yoshikiyo|1=Minamoto no Yoshikiyo}} (1075–1149), son of Yoshimitsu, was the first to take the name of Takeda, which he took when his father granted him Takeda domain in {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|WD=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi Province|1=Hitachi Province}}; thereafter, he was known as Takeda Yoshikiyo. ===Kamakura to early Azuchi–Momoyama periods=== In the 12th century, at the end of the Heian period, the Takeda family-controlled {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}}. Along with a number of other families, they supported their cousin [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] against the [[Taira clan|Taira]] clan in the {{ill|Genpei War|en|Genpei War|WD=Q737542|lt=Genpei War|1=Genpei War}} (1180–85). When Yoritomo was first defeated at Ishibashiyama (1181), {{ill|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|en|Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)|WD=Q7392303|lt=Takeda Nobuyoshi|1=Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186)}} (1128–86) was applied for help, and the Takeda sent an army of 25,000 soldiers to support Yoritomo. Takeda Nobumitsu (1162–1248), son of Nobuyoshi, fought against the Taira, against {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|en|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|WD=Q1139202|lt=Kiso Yoshinaka|1=Minamoto no Yoshinaka}} (1184), distinguished himself in the [[:en:Battle of Ichinotani|Battle of Ichinotani]] (1184), and was appointed ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' (Governor) of Kai province. He also fought against the {{ill|Northern Fujiwara|en|Northern Fujiwara|WD=Q1050942|lt=Northern Fujiwara|1=Northern Fujiwara}} (1189) and against {{ill|Wada Yoshimori|en|Wada Yoshimori|WD=Q3564968|lt=Wada Yoshimori|1=Wada Yoshimori}} (1213). During the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}}, he helped the {{ill|Hōjō clan|en|Hōjō clan|WD=Q834364|lt=Hōjō|1=Hōjō clan}}, and led 50,000 soldiers as 'Daishōgun of the Tosando' , and in reward received the governorship of Aki province (1221). Takeda Nobuhide (1413–40), eldest son of the Takeda Nobushige (1390–1465), Shugo of Aki, helped the 6th shogun {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshinori|en|Ashikaga Yoshinori|WD=Q239170|lt=Ashikaga Yoshinori|1=Ashikaga Yoshinori}} (1394–1441) against the revolt of Isshiki Yoshitsura and was granted the governorship of Wakasa province (1440). Takeda Nobukata (1420–71) inherited the titles of Shugo of Wakasa from his brother Nobuhide, and that of Shugo of Aki from his father Nobushige. During the {{ill|Ōnin War|en|Ōnin War|WD=Q385676|lt=Ōnin War|1=Ōnin War}} (1467–77) he occupied Tango province that belonged to Isshiki Yoshinao and received the governorship of Tango province (1469). His brother Takeda Kuninobu (1437–90) inherited the titles of Shugo of Aki, Wakasa, and Tango provinces, but lost Tango in 1474. Until the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the Takeda were Shugo of the provinces of Kai (since Yoritomo), {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|WD=Q965029|lt=Aki|1=Aki Province}} (since 1221), and {{ill|Wakasa Province|en|Wakasa Province|WD=Q1053713|lt=Wakasa|1=Wakasa Province}} (since 1440).{{Citation needed |date=May 2020}} ===Sengoku period=== {{Campaignbox Campaigns of the Takeda}} Immediately prior to the Sengoku period, the Takeda helped to suppress the Rebellion of Uesugi Zenshū (1416–1417).{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Uesugi Zenshū, Rebellion of | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} {{ill|Uesugi Zenshū|en|Uesugi Zenshū|WD=Q7877480|lt=Uesugi Zenshū|1=Uesugi Zenshū}} (d. 1417) was the ''{{ill|Kanrei|en|Kanrei|WD=Q1202497|lt=Kanrei|1=Kanrei}}'' chief advisor to {{ill|Ashikaga Mochiuji|en|Ashikaga Mochiuji|WD=Q4805073|lt=Ashikaga Mochiuji|1=Ashikaga Mochiuji}}, an enemy of the central {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|WD=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate|1=Ashikaga shogunate}} and the {{ill|Kantō kubō|en|Kantō kubō|WD=Q860777|lt=Kantō kubō|1=Kantō kubō}} governor-general of the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region|1=Kantō region}}. Mochiuji, lord of the [[Uesugi clan]], made a reprisal against the Takeda clan in 1415. This reprisal began a rivalry between the [[Uesugi clan|Uesugi]] and Takeda clans which would last roughly 150 years until the destruction of the Takeda clan at the end of the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Uesugi family | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} While this rivalry existed, the {{ill|Takeda clan (Aki)|en|Takeda clan (Aki)|WD=Q2026427|lt=Takeda|1=Takeda clan (Aki)}} and the [[Uesugi clan|Uesugi]] still had a huge amount of respect for one another. ===Takeda Shingen=== [[File:Komoro castle04s3872.jpg|220px|right|thumb|Komoro Castle, a Takeda clan's castle in Shinano province]] {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Harunobu|1=Takeda Shingen}} (1521 – 1573) succeeded his father Nobutora in 1540 and became ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' lord of {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}} in present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|WD=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}}. In this period the Takeda began to quickly expand from their base in Kai Province. In 1559, Harunobu changed his name to the better-known Takeda Shingen. He faced the {{ill|Later Hōjō clan|en|Later Hōjō clan|WD=Q431928|lt=Hōjō clan|1=Later Hōjō clan}} a number of times, and most of his expansion was to the north, where he fought his most famous battles against {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|en|Uesugi Kenshin|WD=Q311080|lt=Uesugi Kenshin|1=Uesugi Kenshin}}. This series of regional skirmishes is known as the {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battles of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}}. The battles began in 1553, and the best known and severest among them was fought on September 10, 1561.{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Japan | title = Takeda Shingen | url = http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | access-date = 2012-05-17 | year = 2012 | publisher = Shogakukan | location = Tokyo | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ | archive-date = 2007-08-25 }} Shingen is famous for his tactical genius, and innovations, though some historians have argued that his tactics were not particularly impressive nor revolutionary. Nevertheless, Shingen is perhaps most famous for his use of the {{ill|Cavalry|en|Cavalry|WD=Q47315|lt=Cavalry|1=Cavalry}} charge at the {{ill|Battle of Mikatagahara|en|Battle of Mikatagahara|WD=Q690464|lt=Battle of Mikatagahara|1=Battle of Mikatagahara}}. The strength of Shingen's new tactic became so famous that the Takeda army came to be known as the ''Kiba Gundan'' (騎馬軍団), or 'mounted army'. Up until the mid-16th century and Shingen's rise to power, mounted ''samurai'' were primarily archers. There was already a trend at this time towards larger {{ill|infantry|en|infantry|WD=Q29171|lt=infantry|1=Infantry}}-based armies, including a large number of foot archers. In order to defeat these missile troops, Shingen transformed his ''samurai'' from {{ill|Archery|en|Archery|WD=Q108429|lt=archer|1=Archery}}s to {{ill|lancer|en|lancer|WD=Q1045848|lt=lancer|1=Lancer}}s. ===Decline of the Takeda clan=== [[File:Koshukin.jpg|thumb|Gold coin of the Takeda clan of Kai (also called {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kōshū|1=Kai Province}} (甲州金)) in the 16th century, an early example of {{ill|Japanese currency|en|Japanese currency|WD=Q6158487|lt=Japanese currency|1=Japanese currency}} ]] Shingen died on May 13, 1573, at age 53 from illness.{{cite book | last = E. Deal | first = William | authorlink = | title = Handbook to Life in Medieval and Early Modern Japan | publisher = Oxford University Press US | year = 2007 | location = | pages = 44–45 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=DY0XiflmVIAC | isbn = 978-0-19-533126-4}} His son [[Takeda Katsuyori]] (1546–1582) effectively succeeded Shingen though the nominal head of the family was his grandson Takeda Nobukatsu; Katsuyori continued Shingen's aggressive expansion plan south and westward and was initially successful, briefly achieving the largest extent of Takeda rule. However, he was defeated in the {{ill|Battle of Nagashino|en|Battle of Nagashino|WD=Q428369|lt=Battle of Nagashino|1=Battle of Nagashino}} in 1575 by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|WD=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga|1=Oda Nobunaga}} and {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}. After Nagashino, the Takeda clan fell into sharp decline as it had lost many of its most notable samurai during the battle. Katsuyori's position within the clan also became precarious (as he did not fully inherit the clan leadership position); in 1582, two of his relatives defected to the Oda/Tokugawa alliance and Nobunaga succeeded in destroying the Takeda clan shortly thereafter. The campaign saw most of the Takeda followers simply abandoning Katsuyori and the other Takeda family members to their fate. The clan was effectively eliminated, although descendants of the Takeda clan would take prominent positions in the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], established in 1603. ==Modern period== Takeda is also a fairly common family name in modern Japan, though it is unlikely that everyone with the Takeda name is descended from this noble house (several divisions of the family have the Takeda name). In fact, most of the real descendants of the Takeda had a different name when they created a cadet branch. It is also acknowledged that members of the clan married into other Japanese families. During the [[:en:Tokugawa period|Tokugawa period]], several ''daimyō'' families were direct descendants of the Takeda. In 1868, these ''daimyō'' families were : * The {{ill|Matsumae clan|en|Matsumae clan|WD=Q1061883|lt=Matsumae|1=Matsumae clan}}, descendants of Takeda Nobuhiro (1431-1494), son of Takeda Nobukata (1420-1471) of the Aki Takeda. They were ''daimyō'' of Matsumae, the only feudal fief (''[[:en:Han (country subdivision)|han]]'') of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]]. * The {{ill|Nanbu clan|en|Nanbu clan|WD=Q2975330|lt=Nanbu|1=Nanbu clan}}, descendants of Takeda Mitsuyuki (1165-1236), grandson of Takeda Kiyomitsu (1110-1168), established himself at Nambu ({{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|WD=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}}) and took that name. The Nambu were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Morioka Domain|en|Morioka Domain|WD=Q908854|lt=Morioka|1=Morioka Domain}}, of {{ill|Shichinohe Domain|en|Shichinohe Domain|WD=Q7884520|lt=Shichinohe|1=Shichinohe Domain}} and {{ill|Hachinohe Domain|en|Hachinohe Domain|WD=Q7884927|lt=Hachinohe|1=Hachinohe Domain}} ({{ill|Mutsu Province|en|Mutsu Province|WD=Q907389|lt=Mutsu Province|1=Mutsu Province}}). * The {{ill|Yanagisawa clan|en|Yanagisawa clan|WD=Q11534410|lt=Yanagisawa|1=Yanagisawa clan}}, descendants of Takeda Nobunaga, a grandson of Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128-1186), were ''daimyō'' of Kōriyama ({{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}}), of {{ill|Kurokawa Domain|en|Kurokawa Domain|WD=Q849395|lt=Kurokawa|1=Kurokawa Domain}} and {{ill|Mikkaichi Domain|en|Mikkaichi Domain|WD=Q849472|lt=Mikkaichi|1=Mikkaichi Domain}} ({{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}}). * The {{ill|Yonekura clan|en|Yonekura clan|WD=Q2975397|lt=Yonekura|1=Yonekura clan}}, descendants of Takeda Kiyomitsu, settled at Koiwasuji Yonekura and took the name Yonekura. They were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Mutsuura Domain|en|Mutsuura Domain|WD=Q3034502|lt=Mutsuura Domain|1=Mutsuura Domain}} (Musashi province) * The Gotō, descendants of Takeda Nobuhiro, were ''daimyō'' of Gotō (the {{ill|Gotō Islands|en|Gotō Islands|WD=Q1333790|lt=Gotō Islands|1=Gotō Islands}} in {{ill|Hizen Province|en|Hizen Province|WD=Q906926|lt=Hizen Province|1=Hizen Province}}). * The {{ill|Ogasawara clan|en|Ogasawara clan|WD=Q2975340|lt=Ogasawara|1=Ogasawara clan}} are also a cadet branch of the Takeda, by Takeda Nagakiyo (1162–1242), grandson of Takeda Kiyomitsu (1110-1168), and the first to take the name of Ogasawara. His descendants were ''{{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|WD=Q1141023|lt=Shugo|1=Shugo}}'' (governors) of {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|WD=Q289250|lt=Shinano|1=Shinano Province}} and {{ill|Hida Province|en|Hida Province|WD=Q1056535|lt=Hida Province|1=Hida Province}}s, and during the 16th century were at war with their Takeda cousins. In 1868, they were ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Kokura Domain|en|Kokura Domain|WD=Q1140943|lt=Kokura|1=Kokura Domain}}, of Chikuza ({{ill|Buzen Province|en|Buzen Province|WD=Q1047134|lt=Buzen Province|1=Buzen Province}}), of Ashi ({{ill|Harima Province|en|Harima Province|WD=Q1047523|lt=Harima Province|1=Harima Province}}), of {{ill|Karatsu Domain|en|Karatsu Domain|WD=Q743925|lt=Karatsu|1=Karatsu Domain}} (Hizen Province), and of {{ill|Echizen-Katsuyama Domain|en|Echizen-Katsuyama Domain|WD=Q10863286|lt=Katsuyama|1=Echizen-Katsuyama Domain}} (Echizen Province). In 1868, two branches named Takeda were also Ranked among the ''{{ill|Kōke|en|Kōke|WD=Q11669183|lt=Kōke|1=Kōke}}'' (the High Families). This title was given to descendants of great dispossessed ''[[daimyo]]'' families of the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}} to {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}} such as the Takeda, the {{ill|Kyōgoku clan|en|Kyōgoku clan|WD=Q2975299|lt=Kyōgoku|1=Kyōgoku clan}}, the {{ill|Rokkaku clan|en|Rokkaku clan|WD=Q2975342|lt=Rokkaku|1=Rokkaku clan}}, the {{ill|Ōtomo clan|en|Ōtomo clan|WD=Q1096662|lt=Ōtomo|1=Ōtomo clan}}, the [[Toki clan|Toki]], the {{ill|Isshiki clan|en|Isshiki clan|WD=Q11353128|lt=Isshiki|1=Isshiki clan}} and the [[Hatakeyama clan|Hatakeyama]] clans. They received a pension from the shogunate and had privileged missions confided to them. == Cadet branches == [[File:Satoukanayamajou01.JPG|left|thumb|Site of Kanayama Castle (Hiroshima Prefecture), a huge mountain castle surrounded by 50 {{ill|Kuruwa|en|Kuruwa|WD=Q6447542|lt=Kuruwa|1=Kuruwa}} (castle defense walls), on top of the 411m of Mt Takeda, built at the end of the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, the seat of the Aki Takeda]] [[File:Mariyatsu-Castle Senjyojiki.JPG|left|thumb|Site of Mariyatsu Castle ([[:en:Kisarazu, Chiba|Kisarazu]], {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|WD=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}), Koguchi (entrance of castle), the seat of the Kazusa Takeda]] Three major cadet branches of the Takeda clan were established across Japan, along with several smaller branches. Due to the establishment of these cadet branches, the main Takeda clan in Kai Province is also referred to as the Kai Takeda clan. ===Aki Takeda=== The [[:en:Aki Takeda clan|Aki Takeda clan]], established in {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|WD=Q965029|lt=Aki Province|1=Aki Province}} in the present-day western part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}}. Takeda Nobumitsu (1162–1248), Shugo of Kai, received the governorship of Aki province in 1221. [[Takeda Nobutake]] († 1362) was the last Takeda ''Shugo'' of the two provinces of Kai and Aki. His elder son Nobunari received Kai and the younger Ujinobu received Aki province. ===Wakasa Takeda=== The Aki Takeda was granted the governorship of Wakasa province in 1440. The Wakasa Takeda clan was established in {{ill|Wakasa Province|en|Wakasa Province|WD=Q1053713|lt=Wakasa Province|1=Wakasa Province}} in present-day southern {{ill|Fukui Prefecture|en|Fukui Prefecture|WD=Q133879|lt=Fukui Prefecture|1=Fukui Prefecture}}, and separates from Aki province in 1500, when Takeda Motonobu (1461-1521) ruled Wakasa, while his uncle Takeda Mototsuna (1441-1505) ruled Aki. The Wakasa Takeda were known for their patronage of the arts and developing the Takeda school of military etiquette. ===Kazusa Takeda=== The Kazusa Takeda clan, established at the beginning of the Sengoku period in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en|Kazusa Province|WD=Q1055394|lt=Kazusa Province|1=Kazusa Province}} in the present-day central area of {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|WD=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}. Along with the {{ill|Satomi clan|en|Satomi clan|WD=Q2975367|lt=Satomi clan|1=Satomi clan}} of {{ill|Awa Province (Chiba)|en|Awa Province (Chiba)|WD=Q1053044|lt=Awa Province|1=Awa Province (Chiba)}} in the southern part of present-day Chiba Prefecture the two clans replaced the dominance of the [[Chiba clan]] in the region. The Kazusa Takeda is also known as the Mariyatsu Takeda, a reference to their base of power, Mariyatsu Castle. ==Clan literature== The ''Kōshū Hatto'', composed at some point in the 15th century, is the code of law of the Takeda family,{{Cite book|last=Ikegami|first=Eiko|title=The Taming of the Samurai: Honorific Individualism and the Making of Modern Japan|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=1997|isbn=978-0-674-25466-4|language=en}} while the ''{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|en|Kōyō Gunkan|WD=Q586111|lt=Kōyō Gunkan|1=Kōyō Gunkan}}'', composed largely by {{ill|Kōsaka Masanobu|en|Kōsaka Masanobu|WD=Q2477835|lt=Kōsaka Masanobu|1=Kōsaka Masanobu}} in the mid-16th century, is an {{ill|Epic poetry|en|Epic poetry|WD=Q37484|lt=epic poem|1=Epic poetry}} recording the family's history and Shingen's innovations in military tactics. ==Notable figures of the Takeda clan== Among the notable members of the Takeda clan was {{ill|Takeda Nobushige|en|Takeda Nobushige|WD=Q1350640|lt=Takeda ==Popular culture== Takeda is a playable faction in ''{{ill|Shogun: Total War|en|Shogun: Total War|WD=Q528310|lt=Shogun: Total War|1=Shogun: Total War}}'' and ''[[:en:Shogun 2|Shogun 2]]''. The Takeda clan in feudal Japan is in the manga and the anime of ''{{ill|Inuyasha|en|Inuyasha|WD=Q182056|lt=Inuyasha|1=Inuyasha}}''. Takeda Shingen and his peasant {{ill|Doppelgänger|en|Doppelgänger|WD=Q461363|lt=Doppelgänger|1=Doppelgänger}} are the main subjects of ''{{ill|Kagemusha|en|Kagemusha|WD=Q854990|lt=Kagemusha|1=Kagemusha}}'', directed by {{ill|Akira Kurosawa|en|Akira Kurosawa|WD=Q8006|lt=Akira Kurosawa|1=Akira Kurosawa}}.
